abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major global health burden, and renal fibrosis is a common pathological correlate of progressive loss of kidney function. Renal tubular epithelial cells (RTECs), particularly proximal tubular epithelial cells (PTECs), contain abundant mitochondria and depend on oxidative metabolism to support solute transport. This metabolic specialization renders them vulnerable to hypoxia, lipotoxicity, uremic toxins, aging, inflammation, and hemodynamic stress. Persistent mitochondrial injury can suppress fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation, deplete nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, increase mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, destabilize mitochondrial DNA, and disrupt biogenesis, dynamics, mitochondria-associated membrane signaling, and mitophagy. These abnormalities promote maladaptive repair, senescence, inflammatory cell death, and paracrine signaling to fibroblasts, macrophages, endothelial cells, and pericytes. Evidence is organized within a tubule-to-niche framework that distinguishes causal perturbation from temporal or transcriptomic association, model-specific findings from cross-model convergence, and experimental efficacy from clinical translation. Single-cell, spatial, and organoid studies are considered alongside evidence from human biopsy specimens and biomarkers. Mitochondrial dysfunction is thus treated as a context-dependent contributor to, and amplifier of, CKD-associated fibrotic remodeling rather than a universal initiating event. Although strategies targeting bioenergetics, redox balance, mitochondrial quality control, and tubular delivery are promising, translation is constrained by disease heterogeneity, intervention timing, target specificity, pharmacokinetics, and the scarcity of validated human antifibrotic endpoints.

Conflict of interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Institutional review board statement: Not applicable. This study is a narrative review and did not involve human participants or animal subjects. Informed consent statement: Not applicable. Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the writing process: The initial draft of this manuscript was written independently by the authors. ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used solely to translate and polish the English language of the author-written draft, limited to improving grammar, wording, and readability. All text generated by the tool was reviewed and revised sentence by sentence by the authors. All academic viewpoints, study design, data analysis, and conclusions are the sole responsibility of the authors. No AI-assisted tool was used to generate oranalyze study data. The tool was not involved in appraising the literature search results; all references were verified by the authors against the original sources. Literature search strategy: PubMed/MEDLINE and Crossref were searched from database inception through 10 June 2026. Search terms included combinations of “chronic kidney disease” or “renal fibrosis” with “renal tubular epithelial cell”, “proximal tubule”, “mitochondria”, “fatty acid oxidation”, “oxidative phosphorylation”, “NAD⁺”, “mitophagy”, “mitochondrial dynamics”, “mitochondria-associated membrane”, “mtDNA”, “inflammasome”, “single-cell”, “spatial transcriptomics”, “organoid”, “biomarker”, or intervention-specific terms. English-language original studies, human biopsy and clinical studies, multi-omic datasets, and authoritative reviews were considered, with a focus on literature published during 2021–2026. Reference lists were hand-searched, and supplementary targeted searches conducted during manuscript development identified additional studies that substantially informed the synthesis. As a narrative review, study selection and evidence synthesis were qualitative; no formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis was
